title: JS Engine & Memory Internals
description: V8/SpiderMonkey internals, execution contexts, call stack limits, lexical environments, TDZ, and 'this' binding mechanics.

subtopics.title: Execution Context & Call Stack
subtopics.summary: Creation phase vs Execution phase, Global Execution Context, Function Context, and Stack Overflow mechanics.
subtopics.mentalModel: Before running any code line, the JS engine allocates memory for declarations (Creation Phase), setting up variable records and the [[Environment]] reference. In the Execution Phase, code is evaluated line-by-line synchronously onto the single-threaded Call Stack.
subtopics.traps: Variable shadowing, deep recursive calls exhausting stack space (RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded), and context creation cost.

questions.title: Call Stack Depth Calculator
questions.concept: Call Stack Execution & Linear Frame Tracking
questions.problemStatement: Implement a function `measureStackDepth(limit)` that calculates how many nested function calls can be made synchronously without overflowing the stack. If `limit` is reached, it should return the count of frames reached safely.
questions.interviewTrap: Attempting an unbounded recursion will crash with RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. In production you must establish guard rails.

testCases.name: Reaches small depth of 10 frames
testCases.testFn: return measureStackDepth(10);

testCases.name: Reaches depth of 500 frames safely
testCases.testFn: return measureStackDepth(500);

testCases.name: Handles limit of 0 correctly
testCases.testFn: return measureStackDepth(0);

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: The JavaScript Call Stack is a LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) data structure maintained by the runtime host (e.g. V8 in Chrome/Node.js, JavaScriptCore in Safari) to manage execution contexts. When a function is invoked, a new Function Execution Context frame is pushed onto the stack containing its Lexical Environment, Variable Environment, and 'this' binding. When the function returns, its frame is popped.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Initialize a linear depth counter starting at 0.
Define an inner recursive function `recurse()` representing single call-frame allocations.
Check guard condition: if the current depth is greater than or equal to `limit`, terminate immediately and return the reached depth without allocating further stack frames.
Increment the frame counter, invoke `recurse()` to push the next frame onto the engine's call stack, and return the unwound result.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In V8, call stack size is governed by internal thread stack memory (typically ~1MB in Node.js and ~10,000 to 12,000 frames depending on local variable payload sizes). Without a terminal guard, unbounded recursion exhausts stack pointer boundaries and triggers 'RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded'. This function demonstrates linear frame allocation with explicit memory safety limits.

complexity.time: O(N) where N is min(limit, maxStackDepth), executing one synchronous activation record push per step.
complexity.space: O(N) stack memory allocations for N nested call frames on the engine call stack.

edgeCasesHandled: limit = 0 immediately returns 0 without pushing any recursive frames.
Large safe limits (e.g. 500) run within normal engine call stack bounds without overflowing.
Explicit guard preventing infinite recursion and V8 call stack overflow.

specifications: ECMA-262 §9.4 Execution Contexts (Standard specification of running execution context stack)
V8 Engine Source: v8/src/execution/isolate.cc (Stack guard implementation and stack overflow limits)
MDN Web Docs: Call Stack (Runtime execution mechanism)
verifiedRules: ECMA-262 states the execution context stack is used to track execution contexts; the running execution context is always the top element.
Stack exhaustion triggers an implementation-defined RangeError as verified across V8 and SpiderMonkey.

questions.title: Fix Deep Stack Overflow (Trampoline / Iterative Traversal)
questions.concept: Tail-Call Trampolining & Heap vs Stack Allocation
questions.problemStatement: A standard recursive traversal of a deep linked list crashes with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` for large N. Implement `safeTraverse(head)` that iterates through the list without exhausting the call stack, returning the total count of nodes.
questions.interviewTrap: Candidates often write simple recursion `count(node.next) + 1` which overflows around 10,000 calls in V8. Converting to an iterative loop or trampoline moves frames from call stack to heap memory.

testCases.name: Counts 3-node linked list
testCases.testFn: const list = { val: 1, next: { val: 2, next: { val: 3, next: null } } }; return safeTraverse(list);

testCases.name: Handles null head without error
testCases.testFn: return safeTraverse(null);

testCases.name: Traverses 30,000 nodes without stack overflow
testCases.testFn: let head = null; for(let i = 0; i < 30000; i++) { head = { val: i, next: head }; } return safeTraverse(head);

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Standard recursion accumulates stack frames linearly, causing a stack overflow (RangeError) for deep trees or large collections. The Trampoline pattern and iterative stack traversal transform recursive algorithm control flows into an iterative loop, trading call stack frames for heap-allocated thunk closures or arrays.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Replace synchronous deep recursive tree traversal with an explicit heap-allocated stack: `const stack = [root]`.
Loop synchronously while the heap stack is non-empty (`while (stack.length > 0)`).
Pop the current node from the stack, accumulate its value into the sum accumulator.
Push its right and left children onto the stack to preserve traversal order.
Return the accumulated sum once the queue is exhausted, consuming O(1) call stack frames.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: Engines allocate memory for call frames on the thread's fixed-size execution stack (typically 1MB). In contrast, the JavaScript memory heap can grow dynamically to gigabytes (bounded by `--max-old-space-size`). Iterative traversal completely bypasses stack overflow limitations by keeping data on the heap.

complexity.time: O(N) where N is the total number of nodes in the binary tree.
complexity.space: O(D) heap space where D is the maximum depth of the tree (O(1) Call Stack space).

edgeCasesHandled: Empty tree (root === null or undefined) returns 0 safely.
Extremely deep linear trees (e.g., 20,000 degenerate left-child nodes) process smoothly without stack overflow.
Standard multi-branch binary trees calculate exact sums.

specifications: ECMA-262 §15.10 Tail Call Optimization (Note: TCO is only supported in strict mode JavaScriptCore; V8 dropped syntactic TCO, necessitating trampolining/iteration)
V8 Blog: Tail Call Optimization analysis and heap-based trampolining
verifiedRules: Heap-based iteration eliminates recursive activation record allocation on the V8 C++ stack.
Iterative traversal is the standard production design pattern for AST walkers in Babel and TypeScript compiler.

questions.title: Synchronous Execution Context Profiler
questions.concept: Execution Context Call Tracking & Stack Unwinding
questions.problemStatement: Build an execution context tracker `createExecutionTracker()` that returns an object with methods: `enter(contextName)`, `exit(contextName)`, `getCurrentContext()`, and `getCallStackSnapshot()`. It must validate that exiting matches the current active top of the call stack (LIFO order), and throw an Error if an unmatched exit occurs.
questions.interviewTrap: Forgetting that call stacks are strictly LIFO (Last-In First-Out). Exiting a parent before a child context indicates invalid unnesting.

testCases.name: Tracks nested contexts in LIFO order
testCases.testFn: const t = createExecutionTracker(); t.enter('Global'); t.enter('fnA'); return t.getCurrentContext();

testCases.name: Unwinds stack accurately on exit
testCases.testFn: const t = createExecutionTracker(); t.enter('Global'); t.enter('fnA'); t.exit('fnA'); return t.getCurrentContext();

testCases.name: Throws error on mismatched exit
testCases.testFn: const t = createExecutionTracker(); t.enter('A'); try { t.exit('B'); return false; } catch (e) { return true; }

details.name: Tracks nested contexts in LIFO order

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A synchronous Execution Context Profiler wraps function invocations to track execution timelines, call tree nesting depth, execution duration, and return values without perturbing synchronous control flow.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Maintain internal state: `currentDepth` counter and an array of logged `records`.
When profiling a function, record `startTime = performance.now()` and snapshot `depth = currentDepth`.
Increment `currentDepth++` to denote a nested child execution context.
Execute the target function within a `try...finally` block to guarantee decrementing `currentDepth--` even if an exception is thrown.
In `finally`, measure `endTime = performance.now()`, push `{ name, duration: endTime - startTime, depth, result }` to log, and return the result.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: This mirrors how devtools profilers (like the Chrome DevTools CPU profiler and Node.js `async_hooks` / PerformanceObserver) record flame charts. The `try...finally` construct guarantees lexical stack unwinding regardless of whether the context terminates via normal completion or abrupt completion.

complexity.time: O(1) profiling overhead per function invocation + execution time of target function.
complexity.space: O(K) heap memory where K is the number of profiled function invocations.

edgeCasesHandled: Deeply nested function calls correctly track depth increments (0 -> 1 -> 2).
Functions that throw errors still properly unwind `currentDepth`.
Zero-duration or microsecond-precision function calls are measured using high-resolution performance timers.

specifications: W3C High Resolution Time Level 3 (performance.now() precision and monotonic clock)
ECMA-262 §9.4.1 Execution Context Completion Records (Abrupt vs Normal completions)
verifiedRules: The profiler faithfully reflects the LIFO lifecycle of activation records.
`try...finally` guarantees stack state integrity under ECMA-262 §14.15.

subtopics.title: Scope Chain, Lexical Scoping & Closures
subtopics.summary: Lexical environments, outer scope references, closures in loops, and memory leak retention.
subtopics.mentalModel: Functions in JS carry an internal [[Environment]] slot pointing to their lexical parent. A closure is formed whenever an inner function survives outside its parent scope while retaining references to variables in that parent's Lexical Environment Record.
subtopics.traps: The classic loop trap `for(var i=0; i<3; i++) setTimeout(...)`, retaining large objects in closure scope unintentionally, and stale closures in callbacks.

questions.title: Private Counter Factory with Step
questions.problemStatement: Implement `createCounter(initialValue, step)` that encapsulates `initialValue` and `step` in a closure. It returns an object with `increment()`, `decrement()`, `getValue()`, and `reset()`.
questions.interviewTrap: Exposing internal variables directly or allowing external mutation without getters/setters.

testCases.name: Increments and decrements with step
testCases.testFn: const c = createCounter(10, 5); return c.increment();

testCases.name: Independent counters maintain isolated states
testCases.testFn: const c1 = createCounter(0, 1); const c2 = createCounter(10, 2); c1.increment(); return [c1.getValue(), c2.getValue()];

testCases.name: Resets accurately to initial value
testCases.testFn: const c = createCounter(5, 2); c.increment(); c.increment(); c.reset(); return c.getValue();

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A closure is the combination of a function bundled together with references to its surrounding lexical environment ([[Environment]]). A private counter factory uses closures to encapsulate state variables away from global scope, exposing only controlled modifier functions.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Initialize private variable `count = initial` and `stepValue = step` inside factory function.
Return an object containing accessor and mutator methods: `increment()`, `decrement()`, `reset()`, and `get()`.
Each method maintains a live reference to `count` and `stepValue` through the outer lexical environment record.
Outside consumers cannot read or mutate `count` directly, ensuring information hiding.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In V8, variables referenced by an inner function that outlives the outer function call are allocated in a Heap Context rather than on the thread Call Stack. The returned methods hold an internal `[[Scopes]]` pointer referencing this Context object, preventing V8's Garbage Collector from reclaiming it.

complexity.time: O(1) for each method call (increment, decrement, reset, get).
complexity.space: O(1) heap allocation for the shared Lexical Environment context.

edgeCasesHandled: Custom initial values and custom step increments (e.g. initial=10, step=5).
Multiple independent counters maintain separate isolated lexical contexts without cross-contamination.
Reset restores initial count state cleanly.

specifications: ECMA-262 §9.1.1 Declarative Environment Records (Lexical scoping and closure mechanics)
MDN Web Docs: Closures & Lexical Scoping
verifiedRules: Inner functions retain access to outer declarative environment records across ticks.
Variables in a closure escape stack allocation and are preserved in heap-allocated context objects.

questions.title: Secure Store with Memory Release & Deep Snapshot
questions.problemStatement: Create `createSecureStore(initialData)` that stores sensitive data within a closure. Provide `get(key)`, `set(key, value)`, `has(key)`, and `clear()`. Crucially, `get(key)` must return a safe deep copy (so mutating the returned object does not mutate the inner store), and `clear()` must empty the inner map to free memory.
questions.interviewTrap: Returning direct object references from closures allows external callers to mutate private state directly.

testCases.name: Stores and retrieves primitive values
testCases.testFn: const s = createSecureStore(); s.set('token', 'abc'); return s.get('token');

testCases.name: Prevents external mutation of stored objects
testCases.input: Mutating returned object does not affect internal store
testCases.testFn: const s = createSecureStore({ user: { name: 'alice' } }); const u = s.get('user'); u.name = 'hacked'; return s.get('user').name;

testCases.name: clear() wipes stored data completely
testCases.testFn: const s = createSecureStore(); s.set('k', 123); s.clear(); return s.has('k');

details.name: Prevents external mutation of stored objects
details.input: Mutating returned object does not affect internal store

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A Secure Store manages sensitive key-value data with granular access controls, immutable deep snapshots, and an explicit `clear()` / memory release mechanism to prevent lingering references from creating memory leaks.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Store data internally inside a private `Map` enclosed within the factory function.
Provide `set(key, val)` and `get(key)` methods.
`snapshot()` performs a deep clone (via structured clone or recursive deep copy) to prevent external callers from mutating internal store state via reference leaks.
`clear()` invokes `map.clear()`, severing references to all stored keys and values, allowing V8's Garbage Collector to reclaim heap memory.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: If an object reference is returned directly from a closed-over store, external code holds a live pointer to that heap object. Deep cloning isolates the stored reference. Calling `clear()` drops the root references from the closure context, rendering the stored objects unreachable from the GC roots during the next Scavenger or Mark-Sweep GC cycle.

complexity.time: O(1) for get/set/clear; O(S) for snapshot where S is serialized size of data.
complexity.space: O(N) heap memory for stored key-value pairs.

edgeCasesHandled: Mutation of snapshotted objects does not affect the internal store.
Clearing the store resets entry count to 0 and releases object references.
Handling non-primitive objects and nested structures safely.

specifications: ECMA-262 §24.1 Map Objects (Garbage collection eligibility on Map.clear)
V8 Memory Management: V8 Garbage Collector Mark-Sweep and Reachability Trees
verifiedRules: Clearing Map references severs reachability paths from GC roots.
Defensive deep cloning prevents mutable reference aliasing across closure boundaries.

questions.title: Advanced Multi-Key Memoizer with Capacity & TTL
questions.problemStatement: Implement `memoize(fn, { maxAge, maxSize })` which returns a memoized version of `fn`. It must serialize multiple arguments into a deterministic key, respect `maxSize` (LRU eviction when full), and expire entries after `maxAge` milliseconds if provided.
questions.interviewTrap: Using simple objects as caches causes memory leaks over time because entries are never evicted. Using Map with LRU deletion and TTL prevents unbounded memory growth.

testCases.name: Caches computation across repeated calls
testCases.input: memoizedFn called twice only executes target once
testCases.testFn: let calls = 0; const square = memoize((x) => { calls++; return x * x; }); const r1 = square(5); const r2 = square(5); return { calls, result: r2 };

testCases.name: Evicts oldest entry when maxSize is exceeded
testCases.testFn: let calls = 0; const fn = memoize((x) => { calls++; return x; }, { maxSize: 2 }); fn(1); fn(2); fn(3); fn(1); return { calls };

testCases.name: Correctly handles multiple arguments
testCases.testFn: let calls = 0; const add = memoize((a, b) => { calls++; return a + b; }); return [add(2, 3), add(3, 2)];

details.name: Caches computation across repeated calls
details.input: memoizedFn called twice only executes target once

details.name: Evicts oldest entry when maxSize is exceeded

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: An advanced multi-key memoizer caches function call results keyed by serialized arguments, implementing both a Maximum Size (LRU eviction policy) and a Time-To-Live (TTL / maxAge) expiration policy.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Enclose a private `Map` holding `{ value, expiry }` objects indexed by serialized string argument keys.
On call, compute `key = JSON.stringify(args)` and check `cache.has(key)`.
If entry exists and `now < entry.expiry`: delete and re-insert the key to update its recency position in the Map (Map preserves insertion order), then return `entry.value`.
If entry expired, delete it from the cache.
Execute underlying function `fn.apply(this, args)`.
If `cache.size >= maxSize`, evict the least recently used entry (`cache.keys().next().value`).
Set `cache.set(key, { value: result, expiry: now + maxAge })` and return result.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: JavaScript `Map` maintains insertion order according to ECMA-262 §24.1.3. Deleting and immediately re-inserting a key promotes it to the most recently used position in O(1) time. Deleting `cache.keys().next().value` evicts the oldest entry in O(1) time without requiring a doubly-linked list.

complexity.time: O(1) average lookup, insertion, and LRU eviction (plus argument serialization time).
complexity.space: O(maxSize) strictly bounded heap memory, preventing unbounded memory leaks.

edgeCasesHandled: Evicts oldest entry when `maxSize` is reached, ensuring memory bounds.
Expired entries past `maxAge` are treated as cache misses and purged.
Multiple arguments with different orderings/types produce distinct cache keys.

specifications: ECMA-262 §24.1.3 Map.prototype.keys (Guarantee of deterministic insertion-order iteration)
V8 Dev Blog: Optimizing Hash Tables and Map collections in V8
verifiedRules: Map key iteration order is strictly insertion-ordered per ECMA-262.
Deleting and re-inserting provides an O(1) LRU cache implementation without secondary data structures.

subtopics.title: Hoisting & Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)
subtopics.summary: var vs let/const, Function Declarations vs Expressions, and parameter default TDZ.
subtopics.mentalModel: All declarations are hoisted during context creation. However, while `var` is initialized to `undefined`, `let` and `const` remain uninitialized in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) until the evaluator passes their actual declaration line. Accessing them in TDZ throws a ReferenceError.
subtopics.traps: Function declaration inside `if` block (ES6 Annex B semantics), class hoisting (classes are NOT hoisted like functions, they behave like `let`), and default parameter referencing uninitialized variables `(a = b, b = 2) => {}`.

questions.title: Var vs Let Hoisting Analyzer
questions.problemStatement: Implement `analyzeHoisting(varCodeStr)` that inspects a simple code snippet and determines whether accessing a variable before its declaration returns `undefined` (hoisted with var) or throws a `ReferenceError` (hoisted into TDZ with let/const). Return 'INITIALIZED_UNDEFINED' or 'TDZ_REFERENCE_ERROR'.
questions.interviewTrap: Believing that `let` and `const` are not hoisted at all. They ARE hoisted to the top of the block, but stay uninitialized in the TDZ.

testCases.name: var declaration is initialized to undefined
testCases.testFn: return analyzeHoisting('var');

testCases.name: let declaration produces TDZ ReferenceError
testCases.testFn: return analyzeHoisting('let');

testCases.name: const declaration produces TDZ ReferenceError
testCases.testFn: return analyzeHoisting('const');

details.name: var declaration is initialized to undefined

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: In JavaScript execution contexts, variable declarations are processed during the Creation Phase. `var` is hoisted and initialized to `undefined`. In contrast, `let` and `const` are hoisted into the Lexical Environment but remain *uninitialized*. The span of code from block entry until the actual declaration is evaluated is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ).
stepByStepWalkthrough: Analyze code or variable access simulation.
For `var`, access before declaration yields `undefined` without error.
For `let` or `const`, access before declaration throws `ReferenceError: Cannot access variable before initialization`.
Our analyzer parses/evaluates variable lifecycle states: 'hoisted-initialized' for var vs 'tdz-uninitialized' for let/const.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In V8, Environment Records contain bindings with an initialization state flag. When `var` binding is instantiated, V8 assigns the special internal `the_hole` value and immediately overwrites it with `undefined`. For `let`/`const`, the binding is left pointing to `the_hole`. Any bytecode instruction (e.g. `LdaCurrentContextSlot`) encountering `the_hole` triggers a runtime ReferenceError.

complexity.time: O(1) constant time classification of declaration types.

edgeCasesHandled: var declarations inside blocks do not have block scope; they hoist to the function/global boundary.
let/const inside blocks create a new block lexical environment record with its own TDZ.
typeof operator on a TDZ variable throws a ReferenceError (unlike undeclared variables which return 'undefined').

specifications: ECMA-262 §14.3.1 Let and Const Declarations (Static Semantics and TDZ specification)
ECMA-262 §9.1.1.1.6 GetBindingValue (Throws ReferenceError if binding is uninitialized)
MDN Web Docs: Temporal Dead Zone
verifiedRules: Accessing let/const prior to lexical declaration must throw ReferenceError.
Variables declared with var are initialized to undefined upon environment instantiation.

questions.title: Parameter Scope TDZ Resolver
questions.concept: Default Parameter Temporal Dead Zone & Scope Boundary
questions.problemStatement: When default parameters reference each other (e.g. `(a = b, b = 2)`), accessing `b` before its evaluation produces a TDZ ReferenceError. Implement `safeDefaultResolver(params, evaluator)` which receives parameter declarations in order and returns an object `{ valid: boolean, errorParam?: string }` detecting whether any parameter references an uninitialized following parameter.
questions.interviewTrap: Parameter scopes evaluate from left to right. A default parameter can reference previously initialized parameters to its left, but referencing a parameter to its right throws a TDZ ReferenceError.

testCases.name: Valid left-to-right default parameter reference
testCases.testFn: return safeDefaultResolver(['a', 'b'], { a: [], b: ['a'] });

testCases.name: TDZ error when referencing right-hand parameter
testCases.input: a depends on b before b is initialized
testCases.testFn: return safeDefaultResolver(['a', 'b'], { a: ['b'], b: [] });

testCases.name: Independent parameters evaluate safely
testCases.testFn: return safeDefaultResolver(['x', 'y', 'z'], { x: [], y: [], z: [] });

details.name: TDZ error when referencing right-hand parameter
details.input: a depends on b before b is initialized

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: When a function has default parameter values, ECMAScript creates an intermediate Parameter Environment Record distinct from the function body environment record. Parameters are evaluated from left to right, and earlier parameters cannot reference later parameters due to TDZ.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Function parameters initialize in left-to-right order inside the parameter scope.
A default parameter `(a = b, b = 1)` throws `ReferenceError` because `b` is evaluated while still in TDZ.
Conversely, `(b = 1, a = b)` succeeds because `b` is already initialized when `a` is evaluated.
Implement resolver function that validates parameter dependency topological ordering to resolve TDZ conflicts safely.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: ECMA-262 §10.2.11 specifies `FunctionDeclarationInstantiation`. If parameter list contains default expressions, an independent Declarative Environment Record is created for parameters before the body's VariableEnvironment is created. Evaluating an uninitialized parameter slot triggers V8's hole check.

complexity.time: O(P) where P is the number of parameters to evaluate and resolve.

edgeCasesHandled: Forward references `(a = b, b = 2)` correctly detected as TDZ violations.
Valid backward references `(a = 2, b = a)` evaluate smoothly.
Explicit arguments override defaults and avoid TDZ evaluation.

specifications: ECMA-262 §10.2.11 FunctionDeclarationInstantiation (Parameter Scope vs Body Scope)
Babel / TC39 Notes on Parameter Scope and Default Parameters
verifiedRules: Parameters with default values form an intermediate lexical scope.
Referencing a downstream default parameter causes a TDZ ReferenceError.

questions.title: Safe Function Declaration & Hoisting Sandbox
questions.concept: ES6 Annex B Block Scoping for Function Declarations
questions.problemStatement: In ES6+, function declarations inside `if` blocks are block-scoped. Implement `evaluateBlockFunctions(condition, trueFnName, falseFnName)` that executes a simulated block-scoped environment and returns which function is accessible outside the block vs inside.
questions.interviewTrap: In legacy ES5 / non-strict mode, function declarations in blocks were hoisted out into function scope, overwriting each other. In strict mode, they are strictly block scoped.

testCases.name: Executes true branch function correctly
testCases.testFn: return evaluateBlockFunctions(true).insideResult;

testCases.name: Executes false branch function correctly
testCases.testFn: return evaluateBlockFunctions(false).insideResult;

testCases.name: Functions are scoped and execute deterministically
testCases.testFn: const r1 = evaluateBlockFunctions(true); const r2 = evaluateBlockFunctions(false); return typeof r1.insideResult === 'string' && typeof r2.insideResult === 'string';

details.name: Functions are scoped and execute deterministically

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A Hoisting & TDZ Sandbox safely evaluates dynamic code strings containing arbitrary var/let/const and function declarations, capturing TDZ violations and hoisting behaviors without crashing the parent execution context.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Construct an isolated execution scope using `new Function()` with trapped globals.
Instrument the code or catch runtime `ReferenceError`s resulting from premature access to uninitialized bindings.
Distinguish between standard undeclared variables (`ReferenceError: x is not defined`) and TDZ access errors (`ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization`).
Return structured diagnostics detailing hoisted identifiers, TDZ traps encountered, and final return values.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: Function declarations in blocks (Annex B.3.3) have complex legacy hoisting semantics. Top-level function declarations are fully hoisted with their implementation during the Creation phase. `new Function` creates a fresh global-like script context that prevents local scope pollution.

complexity.time: O(E) execution time of evaluated code snippet.

edgeCasesHandled: Catching ReferenceErrors from TDZ reads.
Allowing hoisted function calls before declaration line.
Handling syntax errors vs runtime TDZ reference errors distinctly.

specifications: ECMA-262 Annex B.3.3 Block-Level Function Declarations Web Legacy Compatibility
ECMA-262 §19.2.1.1 Function ( p1, p2, … , pn, body ) (Dynamic function evaluation)
verifiedRules: Function declarations are hoisted with function body definition.
TDZ exceptions are distinct runtime ReferenceErrors originating from uninitialized environment slots.

subtopics.title: 'this' Keyword Mechanics & Binding Rules
subtopics.summary: The 4 binding rules: Default, Implicit, Explicit (`call`/`apply`/`bind`), New, plus Lexical `this` in arrow functions.
subtopics.mentalModel: `this` is NOT author-time; it is runtime call-site dependent (except arrow functions, which capture `this` lexically from their enclosing scope). The precedence order is: new binding > explicit binding > implicit binding > default binding (global or undefined in strict mode).
subtopics.traps: Passing methods as callbacks losing implicit `this`, arrow functions used as object methods or prototype methods, and constructors returning an explicit object overriding the `new` instance.

questions.title: Method Callback Context Binder
questions.concept: Preserving Object Context when Passing Callbacks
questions.problemStatement: When an object method is passed as a callback (e.g., `setTimeout(obj.method)`), implicit `this` is lost. Implement `bindMethod(obj, methodName)` that returns a wrapper function guaranteeing that `methodName` always executes with `obj` as `this`, preserving any forwarded arguments.
questions.interviewTrap: Extracting a method `const fn = obj.method; fn()` invokes `fn` with default binding (undefined in strict mode), losing all object properties.

testCases.name: Preserves object property access
testCases.testFn: const user = { name: 'Antigravity', getName() { return this.name; } }; const bound = bindMethod(user, 'getName'); return bound();

testCases.name: Forwards arguments properly to bound method
testCases.input: bound method passes greeting and punctuation
testCases.testFn: const user = { name: 'Antigravity', greet(prefix, suffix) { return `${prefix}, ${this.name}${suffix}`; } }; const bound = bindMethod(user, 'greet'); return bound('Hello', '!');

testCases.name: Maintains binding even when assigned to another variable
testCases.testFn: const calc = { value: 42, getVal() { return this.value; } }; const detached = bindMethod(calc, 'getVal'); return detached();

details.name: Forwards arguments properly to bound method
details.input: bound method passes greeting and punctuation

details.name: Maintains binding even when assigned to another variable

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: In JavaScript, the value of `this` is determined at call-time by how a function is called (the Call-Site), not where it is declared. Passing an object method as a callback detaches the function from its receiver object, resulting in `this` reverting to `undefined` (in strict mode) or the global object.
stepByStepWalkthrough: A callback context binder takes an object and a method name (or function) and returns a bound function.
Use `method.bind(context)` or an arrow wrapper `(...args) => target.apply(context, args)`.
When the callback is invoked by a third party (e.g. event listener or array method), `this` is hard-bound to the specified context object.
Return the bound callback.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: When invoking `obj.method()`, the MemberExpression produces a Reference Record with base `obj`. The call operation extracts `this` from the Reference base. When passed as a value `callback = obj.method`, the Reference Record is evaluated (GetValue), dropping the base. Binding creates an exotic bound function object storing `[[BoundTargetFunction]]` and `[[BoundThis]]`.

complexity.time: O(1) creation time; O(1) invocation overhead.
complexity.space: O(1) memory for the bound function wrapper.

edgeCasesHandled: Preserves passed arguments forwarded to the bound function.
Guarantees correct `this` even when called with `undefined` or different receiver.
Supports methods relying on object state.

specifications: ECMA-262 §10.4.1.2 Bound Function Exotic Objects
ECMA-262 §13.3.7.1 Runtime Semantics: Evaluation (Call-site reference resolution)

verifiedRules: Passing methods as un-bound callbacks strips the reference record base.
Bound function exotic objects override call-site receiver resolution.

questions.title: Implement Custom Function.prototype.myCall & myApply
questions.concept: Explicit Context Invocation via Property Binding
questions.problemStatement: Implement `myCall(thisArg, ...args)` on `Function.prototype` without using native `.call()`, `.apply()`, or `.bind()`. It must handle null/undefined `thisArg` (falling back to globalThis/window), wrap primitives, and avoid colliding with existing properties on `thisArg` using `Symbol()`.
questions.interviewTrap: Using a plain string key like `context.__fn__ = this` can overwrite existing properties on the target object. Using `Symbol()` guarantees zero key collision.

testCases.name: Invokes function with explicit object context
testCases.testFn: function greet(greeting) { return greeting + ' ' + this.name; } return greet.myCall({ name: 'Bob' }, 'Hi');

testCases.name: Cleans up temporary property after invocation
testCases.input: Verify no lingering properties left on context
testCases.testFn: const ctx = {}; function test() { return 1; } test.myCall(ctx); return Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(ctx).length;

testCases.name: Handles primitive numbers or strings as thisArg
testCases.testFn: function getLen() { return this.length; } return getLen.myCall('hello');

Cleans up temporary property after invocation

details.name: Handles primitive numbers or strings as thisArg

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Implementing custom polyfills for `Function.prototype.myCall` and `Function.prototype.myApply` requires invoking the target function with an explicit `thisContext` without using native `.call()` or `.apply()`.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Attach `myCall(context, ...args)` and `myApply(context, argsArray)` to `Function.prototype`.
Default `context` to `globalThis` if `context` is `null` or `undefined` (in non-strict semantics), or coerce primitives to objects via `Object(context)`.
Create a unique property on the context object using `const fnKey = Symbol('fn')` to prevent overwriting existing keys.
Assign the function to that property: `context[fnKey] = this`.
Invoke the function via property access: `const result = context[fnKey](...args)` (or `...argsArray`).
Delete the temporary property `delete context[fnKey]` in a `try...finally` block to prevent object pollution, then return the result.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: By executing `context[fnKey](...)`, the JavaScript engine constructs a Reference Record whose base is `context`. During evaluation of the call, `this` is automatically set to `context` according to standard property invocation semantics.

complexity.time: O(1) overhead plus execution time of the target function.
complexity.space: O(1) temporary Symbol property on context.

edgeCasesHandled: Primitive contexts (numbers, strings, booleans) wrapped via `Object(context)`.
Null or undefined context defaults to `globalThis`.
`Symbol` property key prevents collisions with existing properties on `context`.
Exceptions during function execution still clean up the temporary property.

specifications: ECMA-262 §20.2.3.1 Function.prototype.apply (Specification of thisArg coercion and arg list evaluation)
ECMA-262 §20.2.3.3 Function.prototype.call
verifiedRules: Non-strict thisArg defaults to global object if null/undefined.
Property call syntax sets `this` to the base of the reference record.

questions.title: Custom 'bind' Polyfill with 'new' Operator Support
questions.concept: Currying, Prototype Chaining, and new.target Resolution
questions.problemStatement: Implement `Function.prototype.myBind(thisArg, ...outerArgs)`. It must support partial application (currying), and when the bound function is invoked as a constructor using `new BoundFn()`, the provided `thisArg` MUST be ignored and a new instance inheriting from the original function's prototype must be created.
questions.interviewTrap: 90% of candidates miss the `new` operator rule: when a bound function is called with `new`, the bound `thisArg` is completely ignored in favor of the newly instantiated object.

testCases.name: Standard bound invocation with curried arguments
testCases.testFn: function add(a, b) { return a + b; } const add10 = add.myBind(null, 10); return add10(20);

testCases.name: Maintains object this context
testCases.testFn: const user = { name: 'Alex' }; function getName() { return this.name; } return getName.myBind(user)();

testCases.name: Supports 'new' operator correctly overriding thisArg
testCases.testFn: function Point(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } const BoundPoint = Point.myBind({ x: 99 }, 5); const pt = new BoundPoint(10); return { x: pt.x, y: pt.y, isInstance: pt instanceof Point };

details.name: Standard bound invocation with curried arguments

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A complete polyfill for `Function.prototype.myBind` must not only bind `this` and partially apply arguments (currying), but also support being used with the `new` operator. When a bound function is constructed (`new boundFn()`), the bound `this` must be IGNORED and a fresh instance of the original constructor must be created instead.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Capture target function: `const targetFn = this`.
Capture bound arguments: `const boundArgs = Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments, 1)`.
Define the bound function: `function bound(...) { ... }`.
Check if called via `new`: `this instanceof bound` (or `new.target`).
If called via `new`, use `this` (the newly instantiated object); otherwise, use the originally supplied `boundThis`.
Concatenate boundArgs with invocation arguments.
Inherit prototype chain: Set `bound.prototype = Object.create(targetFn.prototype)` so instances pass `instanceof targetFn` checks.
Execute `targetFn.apply(effectiveThis, allArgs)` and return result (handling constructor object returns).
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: ECMA-262 §10.4.1.1 specifies `[[Construct]]` on Bound Function Exotic Objects. When constructed via `new`, the bound function delegates to the original constructor's `[[Construct]]`, completely bypassing `[[BoundThis]]`. Our polyfill replicates this specification requirement faithfully.

complexity.time: O(1) creation; O(1) dispatch per call.
complexity.space: O(A) space for bound arguments array.

edgeCasesHandled: Constructor usage (`new boundFn()`) ignores `boundThis` and instantiates target prototype.
Partial application (currying) combines initial arguments with runtime arguments.
Instanceof operator works for both bound and original constructor.

specifications: ECMA-262 §10.4.1.1 [[Construct]] on Bound Function Exotic Objects
ECMA-262 §20.2.3.2 Function.prototype.bind

verifiedRules: new operator overrides bound thisArg per ECMA-262 §10.4.1.1.
